subject: Business Models
title: Dynamic Pricing
description: A short lesson to help you apply Dynamic Pricing.

hook.text: Uber charges $8 at noon and $32 at 2 AM for the same ride. The algorithm sets the price, not the driver.

buildup.text: Dynamic pricing adjusts prices in real-time based on demand, supply, time, weather, or customer data.

discovery.text: Airlines pioneered dynamic pricing in the 1980s. Two passengers on the same flight might pay 10x different fares.

twist.text: Amazon changes prices 2.5 million times per day. Most shoppers never notice the constant fluctuations.

climax.text: Dynamic pricing maximizes revenue but feels unfair. The challenge is transparency—or hiding it well enough.

punchline.text: Same ride, 4x the price at surge. Algorithms set prices, not fairness.

quiz.question: How often does Amazon change its prices?

details.summary: Dynamic pricing adjusts prices in real time based on demand, supply, competition, time, and customer characteristics. Airlines pioneered it with yield management, and today ride-sharing surge pricing, hotel rates, and e-commerce prices all fluctuate algorithmically.
details.whyItMatters: Dynamic pricing captures maximum willingness to pay across different customers and moments. It maximizes revenue from perishable inventory like airline seats and hotel rooms where unsold capacity generates zero revenue.
takeaways: Algorithms adjust prices in real time based on supply and demand signals
Airlines pioneered yield management to maximize revenue per flight
Ride-sharing surge pricing balances supply and demand dynamically

faq.question: How does airline yield management work?
faq.answer: Airlines divide seats into fare classes and adjust availability based on booking pace, historical demand, and competitor pricing. As a flight fills, cheaper fare classes close and only higher-priced seats remain. Last-minute business travelers pay premiums.

faq.question: Why does dynamic pricing sometimes cause customer backlash?
faq.answer: Customers perceive sudden price increases during emergencies or peak demand as exploitative. Uber's surge pricing during severe weather drew criticism. Transparency about pricing logic and caps on maximum multipliers help manage customer expectations.
